title: sre-slos-error-budgets-capacity-and-runbooks-standards-2026-02-15
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview:

This document captures Redwood Inference engineering standards for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and the format and maintenance of SRE runbooks. It is intended as the canonical reference for eng-sre and product teams that own customer-facing services and inference infrastructure.

Goals:
- Define consistent SLOs and error-budget lifecycles across platform and product services.
- Provide a repeatable capacity planning process that ties to SLOs and business growth.
- Standardize incident review artifacts and timelines to accelerate learning.
- Describe operational tooling baseline (dashboards, alerts, tracing) required for service readiness.
- Establish runbook templates and ownership to enable on-call effectiveness.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Intro: SLOs quantify the customer-facing reliability commitments we make. Error budgets (1 - SLO) are the operational resource we burn when the service fails to meet the objective; they drive prioritization between feature work and reliability work.

SLO taxonomy and targets (examples):
- Availability (customer RPCs): 99.95% monthly availability (target for production-hosted inference endpoints).
- Latency (response time): P99 <= 300 ms for small prompt generation routes; P95 <= 120 ms for embedding endpoints.
- Correctness (model output failure): <= 0.1% model-execution errors (e.g., OOM, kernel crash) per month.
- Background jobs: 99.9% success rate per week for scheduled maintenance/ETL pipelines.

Measurement rules:
- Use client-observed metrics as the primary signal for availability/latency SLOs where possible. Fallback signals (infra-health) are secondary and must be documented per-service.
- Windowing: calculate SLO over rolling 28-day windows for operational visibility; report monthly (calendar month) for stakeholder communications.
- Aggregation: SLOs should be defined per customer-tier where behavior differs (hosted vs dedicated). Avoid overly fine-grained per-route SLOs unless high risk.

Error budget policy and lifecycle:
- Error budget = (1 - SLO) * window. E.g., 99.95% availability -> error budget is ~21.6 minutes/month.
- Burn rate alerts:
  - Burn rate > 2x for 1 hour -> page platform SRE lead and create an incident review ticket.
  - Burn rate > 5x sustained for 15 minutes -> engage incident commander and consider throttling or degradations.
- Actions when error budget is exhausted: immediate freeze of non-critical rollouts for affected services, mandatory reliability work item creation, weekly prioritization until budget restores to a healthy state.
- Monthly reviews: product and SRE review per-service SLO adherence and adjust SLOs if customer expectations or architecture changes justify it.

2) Capacity planning

Principles:
- Plan for traffic using demand forecasts tied to product metrics (DAU, active requests/day, token throughput).
- Maintain minimum headroom of 30% on dedicated inference pools for sustained traffic; for bursty workloads target 50% burst capacity via autoscale or overflow routing.
- Use p95/p99 request size and token distributions to model GPU memory and compute needs.

Process (quarterly cadence with monthly refreshes):
1. Forecast inputs (owner: service/product manager): expected growth, planned launches, marketing events.
2. Telemetry review (owner: SRE): actual QTR traffic, p95/p99 sizes, token/sec, KV-cache hit rates.
3. Capacity model (owner: infra capacity): map forecast to GPU-hours and slot counts using current runtime profiles; include quantized and non-quantized variants.
4. Risk & mitigation plan: identify single points of capacity failure, define fallback model variants, and pre-warm critical caches.
5. Approval & budget request (owner: infra/product): submit capacity changes to finance and infra procurement with lead time.

Capacity safety checks and guardrails:
- Autoscaler health: target 95% success rate for scale-up operations within configured SLA (e.g., scale within 120s).
- Pre-warm policy: for scheduled launches (>100% expected increase), pre-warm at least 50% of expected capacity 2 hours prior.
- Spillover routing: define candidate models (smaller quantized variants) for graceful degradation under constrained capacity.

3) Reliability initiatives and prioritization

Initiative types (examples):
- Systemic reliability work: kernel-level optimizations, runtime batching improvements, KV-cache persistence changes.
- Tactical mitigations: adaptive batching, dynamic routing to cheaper regions, circuit breakers for noisy customers.
- Observability investments: high-cardinality tracing for hot paths, synthetic workloads for perf regressions.

Prioritization framework:
- Use a combination of customer impact (active customers affected, revenue-at-risk), error budget status, and technical risk.
- Minimum bar for wide rollout: must include SLO regression test and canary plan.
- Track initiatives in the reliability roadmap with owner, success metrics, and post-deploy evaluation window (30/60/90 days).

Examples of successful initiatives to emulate:
- Intelligent batching: reduced per-token cost by 18% and improved p95 latency by 12% for streaming generation.
- KV prefix caching: cut model forward calls by 25% for high-repeat prompt patterns.

4) Incident review standards

Scope: All Sev2/Sev1 incidents and any event that burns >25% of a service’s monthly error budget must produce a post-incident review.

Timeline and ownership:
- Initial incident report: produced by incident commander within 24 hours (short summary, impact, mitigation).
- Postmortem draft: owner (service oncall) creates draft within 72 hours with timeline and root cause hypothesis.
- RCA and action items: finalized within 7 days with concrete mitigations and owners assigned.
- Follow-up review: 30-day check on action item completion and validation of effectiveness.

Postmortem template (required fields):
- Incident title and ticket ID
- Severity and affected services/customers
- Timeline (ISO timestamps) of key events
- Impact summary (error budget, customer-visible downtime, revenue impact estimate)
- Root cause(s) and contributing factors
- Immediate mitigations and long-term fixes
- Action items (owner, due date, verification steps)
- Lessons learned and detection/mitigation improvements

Blamelessness: Reviews must be blameless; focus on system and process fixes. When a human error is a factor, ensure training and system improvements prevent recurrence.

5) Operational tooling baseline

Required dashboards (per service):
- SLO dashboard: rolling 28-day SLI graphs (availability, latency percentiles), error budget burn chart.
- Health dashboard: infra metrics (GPU utilization, memory, queue length, scheduler latency).
- Errors & logs: top error types in last 7 days, traces sampled for p99 requests.

Alerts and thresholds (examples):
- P95 latency > target for 5m -> SEV3 alert to service Slack channel.
- P99 latency > target for 3m OR availability breach -> SEV2 page to oncall.
- Error budget burn rate > 2x for 1h -> SEV2 page and auto-create incident ticket.
- Autoscaler failures or pre-warm failures -> SEV2 to infra oncall.

Alert hygiene and fatigue reduction:
- All alerts must include expected symptoms, runbook link, and playbook steps.
- Use alert suppression windows for known maintenance.
- Quarterly alert review: remove noisy alerts and tune thresholds; owners required to justify retention.

Tooling integrations (minimum set):
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for long-term retention (90d SLO data).
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry collected to Jaeger/Tempo.
- Logs: ELK or managed logging with 30d retention for prod.
- Incident management: PagerDuty for paging, Jira for postmortem tasks, Confluence for writeups.

6) SRE runbooks (format and maintenance)

Runbook format (required):
- Title, service, runbook owner, last-tested date, severity level covered.
- Quick checklist (1–3 steps) for immediate mitigation.
- Expanded steps with command-line/check commands, dashboards to inspect, and expected responses.
- Escalation path and related playbooks.
- Post-incident notes area for lessons and changes.

Runbook example (snippet):
- Title: inference-api-high-p99-latency
- Owner: eng-sre-inference
- Quick checklist:
  1) Check SLO dashboard: confirm P99 > 300ms for >3m
  2) Verify GPU utilization and queue depth on infra dashboard
  3) If GPUs saturated: trigger spillover policy -> route to quantized-variant model group
- Commands:
  - kubectl get pods -n inference -l service=inference-api
  - curl -sS https://metrics.internal/api/query?metric=p99_latency&service=inference-api
- Escalation:
  - If spillover fails or p99 remains high after 10m -> page infra SEV2 and IC

Maintenance rules:
- Runbooks must be reviewed and smoke-tested at least once per quarter by the owner.
- Each runbook must include a "last-tested" timestamp and a short test procedure.
- Deprecated runbooks should be archived and linked from the service runbook index.

Governance and metrics for SRE effectiveness
- Track mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to mitigate (MTTM) for Sev1/Sev2 incidents; targets: MTTD < 5m, MTTM < 30m for critical infra.
- Track % of services with published SLOs and runbooks (target 100% for production-tagged services).
- Monthly reliability review: SRE leads present error budget burn, capacity risk, and active remediation items to eng leadership.

References and links:
- SLO calculator spreadsheet (internal): /tools/slo-calculator
- Incident postmortem template: /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template
- Capacity model workbook: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning-workbook

Appendix: Quick checklist for a runbook owner
- Ensure SLOs are instrumented and dashboards exist.
- Validate runbook commands work from a bastion account quarterly.
- Confirm oncall rotation includes at least one trained person who can execute the runbook.
- Keep the related incident review ticket and action items linked in the runbook.

Contact and ownership:
- Eng-SRE leads: David Kim (platform reliability), Priya Shah (runtime reliability), Marco Alvarez (capacity & infra).
- For questions about this standard, open an RFC in the eng-sre team channel or contact eng-sre@redwood.com.
